description: A team of 6, Computer Science students at UNIMAS. Our team name comes from a creative combination of all the first letter of our members' surname, which happens to sound similar to “Bak Kut Teh”, a well-known Malaysian dish. We were impressed by an interactive website (https://kprverse.com/) while deciding on the challenge. Then, we decided to take this challenge and try our best to implement something similar, although what we study is more to backend while this is frontend heavy.
summary:
Since the 1960s, NASA has left landers, rovers and instruments on the Moon and Mars. Children mostly hear about today's missions, while the stories of these retired explorers are told mainly in technical websites and papers that young readers find hard to follow. In places like Sarawak, space can also feel beyond children's reach, and many rural schools and homes have limited internet access.

Our solution, ECHO: Abandoned, but Not Forgotten, is a lightweight interactive story website for children aged 9 to 12. Maya and Adam, two fictional astronauts from Sarawak, visit a longhouse to share their childhood dreams of space. In their story, readers discover the seismometer Apollo 11 left on the Moon in 1969 and join an imagined 2100 visit to NASA's InSight lander on Mars. They learn how marsquakes revealed Mars' interior, explore real seismic recordings, find out why InSight's mission ended and take a quiz.

ECHO separates fact from fiction and cites its sources. At about 1 MB, it loads quickly on slow connections and works offline after the first visit, with narration, a text version and reduced motion. It aims to show children, especially in Sarawak, that exploring space is possible for them.
details:
ECHO: Abandoned, but not forgotten

What it does and how it works

When a mission ends, the machine usually stays where it worked. ECHO is an interactive scroll story that brings one of those quiet explorers back to life: NASA's InSight lander, which listened to Mars from 2018 to 2022. It's for children aged about 9 to 15.

The story starts in a longhouse in Sarawak, Malaysia. Ten-year-old Adam sits outside the longhouse, looks up at the red star, and dreams of becoming an astronaut. We see his science book through his eyes, then follow him to Mars in 2100, now an astronaut. Finally he comes home to the longhouse's shared gallery, to tell the children what he found.

As you scroll, one continuous camera travels from the solar system to Apollo 11's seismometer on the Moon (1969), and on to InSight on Mars. It goes underground to show how marsquake waves revealed the layers inside Mars, then back out to InSight's real goodbye in December 2022.

Readers don't just read, they do what InSight's scientists did:

  • Find the waves: drag P-wave and S-wave markers onto InSight's real seismometer recording of marsquake S1222a (May 4, 2022), the biggest ever recorded on another planet. The time gap between them gives the quake's distance, about 2,200 km. Answers are checked against the Marsquake Service's own picks.
  • Listen to Mars: the same recording, played 400× faster so the shaking becomes a sound you can hear.
  • Choose like the team: as dust covers the solar panels, decide which instrument to keep running, then see what NASA really did.
  • Meet more quiet explorers: ten more, from Surveyor 3 to Voyager 1, each with a real NASA photo and source.
  • Check what you learned: a five-question quiz at the end.


There are two ways in. Watch it is a hands-free three-minute film, read aloud with subtitles. The Full story is about 14 minutes and can be scrolled, stepped through or played.

Benefits

  • Real science, not just facts: children use real NASA data to learn how scientists study the inside of a planet without digging.
  • Built for limited internet: many rural schools in Sarawak have weak or no connection. ECHO can be downloaded once and then runs fully offline, on phones, tablets and old laptops.
  • Clear about what's real: every card is labelled Real data, Historical record, Teaching illustration or Fictional future, so readers always know which is which.
  • Accessible: read aloud for readers who need it (including OKU readers), a plain-text version, keyboard and touch controls, and reduced motion.
  • Honours "abandoned" hardware: it shows that a finished mission isn't junk. Its data keeps teaching us.

Intended impact

We want a child in a Sarawak longhouse to see someone like them become an astronaut, and to feel that space science belongs to them too. Through InSight's story they learn three things:

  • How seismology reveals a planet's interior?
  • Why mission ends?
  • Why the equipment left behind still matters?

They also practise a key skill: telling real evidence apart from imagination.

Tools, languages and hardware

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework and no build step, so it runs straight from a file or any web server.
    • hand-made SVG illustrations;
    • three.js (WebGL) for the 3D planets and the Mars landing site.
    • Web Audio API for music and sound effects;
    • Web Speech API for the narration;
    • a service worker for offline use.
  • Data: InSight SEIS data downloaded from the EarthScope (IRIS) archive and processed with Python and ObsPy. NASA photos come from the Image and Video Library, LRO and HiRISE. The Borneo and Sarawak map is from Natural Earth.
  • Workflow: Git and GitHub, Netlify hosting, and automated testing in headless Chrome.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped write the code, the vector illustrations and the narration script. ChatGPT made the planet style reference. Every science fact was checked against NASA sources.
  • Hardware: only our laptops. Users need nothing but a browser.

How it is creative

  • A local hero: NASA's InSight story is told through a child from Sarawak, in a longhouse setting that young Malaysians recognise.
  • One continuous journey: a single camera moves from a longhouse veranda through Adam's science book, out to the solar system and down into Mars's crust.
  • Data you can touch and hear: a real seismogram becomes a game, and a real marsquake becomes a sound.
  • Fiction in service of fact: an imagined 2100 visit makes the history personal, and it's always clearly labelled.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: every fact links to a NASA or peer-reviewed source, listed on the site. Diagrams are marked "not to scale".
  • Audience: short sentences, reading-speed pacing (about 150 words a minute), and activities instead of long text.
  • Access: works offline and on low-end devices, saves battery when nothing is moving, and has read aloud and a text version.
  • Culture: respectful use of longhouse life and Sarawak's place in the story.
  • Licensing: only open or properly credited music, images and data. We dropped a music track whose copyright we couldn't confirm.
  • Honesty: clear labels separating real, historical and imagined content, and an AI-use statement on the site.
